source: Mamede & Schmidt (2023) Deliberate reflection and clinical reasoning: Founding ideas and empirical findings. Med Educ 57:76-85 [origins]
finding: Deliberate reflection (DR) descends from Dewey (reflection as careful consideration of a belief in the light of its grounds) and Schon (reflection is triggered when routine knowing-in-action fails; the practitioner suspends judgement and scrutinises the grounds of the first explanation). DR is a second look at a hypothesis the person already holds.
numbers: Mamede & Schmidt 2004 questionnaire factor analysis of physicians gave five factors: deliberate induction, deliberate deduction, testing of predictions, openness to reflection, meta-reasoning. DR operationalises the first three. Two thirds of reflection papers in six med-ed journals are descriptive. Prakash 2019 found only 23 adequately controlled studies.
limits: Review of mostly their own lab network. Concept paper, not a new experiment.
agent_relevance: S5 revise is a trigger then test loop on an existing hypothesis. Matches G1 (doubt on a signal) and G2 (revise from evidence).

source: Mamede & Schmidt (2023) Deliberate reflection and clinical reasoning: Founding ideas and empirical findings. Med Educ 57:76-85 [procedure]
finding: The DR procedure has fixed steps: state a hypothesis; list findings that support it; list findings that speak against it; list findings that should be present but are absent; name an alternative hypothesis if the first is wrong and repeat; then rank all hypotheses and choose.
numbers: Seven steps (Table 3). Worked case, a 48-year-old man: asthma first, COPD and pulmonary embolism as alternatives, ranked asthma 1, PE 2, COPD 3.
limits: Hypotheses must emerge one at a time from the evidence (bottom-up), not as a pre-written differential.
agent_relevance: Directly usable as an S8 verify template: for, against and expected-but-missing columns per hypothesis, one hypothesis at a time.

source: Mamede, Schmidt & Penaforte (2008) Effects of reflective practice on the accuracy of medical diagnoses. Med Educ 42:468-475
finding: Founding experiment. Brazilian internal medicine residents diagnosed 16 cases (simple or complex) by pattern recognition or by reflective reasoning. No main effect of reflection, but a complexity by mode interaction: reflection helped on complex cases only.
numbers: N=42 residents, 16 cases, within-subjects. Interaction F(1,41)=4.48, P<0.05.
limits: Only the abstract was read (full paper not available). Vignettes hold all information. One country, small N.
agent_relevance: Do not reflect on every item. Gate the second look on difficulty or on a failed check (G1).

source: Mamede et al. (2010) Conscious thought beats deliberation without attention in diagnostic decision-making: at least when you are an expert. Psychol Res 74:586-592
finding: Replication of the complexity by expertise pattern. Doctors did better with conscious deliberation on complex problems; on simple problems mode did not matter. Novices gained only on simple problems and thinking did not help them on complex ones.
numbers: N=34 internal medicine residents plus 50 fourth-year students; 12 cases (6 simple, 6 complex), 4 per condition, 8 min each, within-subjects. Residents on complex cases: conscious thought beat immediate decision t(33)=2.86 p<0.008 and unconscious thought t(33)=3.12 p<0.005. Initial 0.45 (SD 0.33) to final 0.58 (SD 0.27) after analysis, t(33)=3.00 p<0.01. Simple cases: no difference. Students: conscious thought on complex cases was worse than immediate, t(33)=2.08 p<0.05. Interaction mode x expertise F(2,82)=3.35 p<0.04. Two blinded raters, 84% agreement, score 1/0.5/0.
limits: Full text read this session. Conscious condition = give first diagnosis, then list evidence for and against each hypothesis, add at least one alternative, rate likelihoods. Written cases, 8 min cap. Student t-tests report df 33 though n=50 (as printed).
agent_relevance: Reflection amplifies knowledge and does not create it. A weak solver reflecting alone on a hard problem may do worse, so pair the second look with retrieval or an external check (G2, G3).

source: Mamede, van Gog, van den Berge et al. (2010) Effect of availability bias and reflective reasoning on diagnostic accuracy among internal medicine residents. JAMA 304:1198-1203
finding: Prior similar cases primed wrong answers for second-year residents; structured reanalysis countered it.
numbers: N=36 (18 first-year, 18 second-year). Second-years scored 1.55 on look-alike cases vs 2.19 on others (P=.03). First-years showed the reverse (2.03 vs 1.42). Earlier diagnosis repeated 1.44 vs 0.72 times per resident (P=.04). Reflection: second-years 2.03, first-years 2.31 (main effect P=.006).
limits: Abstract only. Reflection phase always came last on the same four cases, so a plain repeat effect is mixed in. Small N.
agent_relevance: Earlier context primes the wrong answer, like carry-over in a long context. A fresh structured recheck repairs it.

source: Schmidt, Mamede, van den Berge, van Gog, van Saase, Rikers (2014) Exposure to media information about a disease can cause doctors to misdiagnose similar-looking clinical cases. Acad Med 89:285-291
finding: Reading a Wikipedia page on a disease caused later misdiagnosis of look-alikes six hours on. Deliberate reflection restored accuracy.
numbers: N=38 residents. Bias-expected cases 0.56 vs bias-not-expected 0.70 (P=.016). Misdiagnosis as the read disease 0.61 when read vs 0.29 when not. After reflection 0.71.
limits: Abstract only. Simulated cases.
agent_relevance: Exposure bias from earlier text is large and a structured recheck undoes it. Supports re-reading the raw case in S8, not reasoning from memory of the first pass.

source: Mamede, Splinter, van Gog, Rikers, Schmidt (2012) Exploring the role of salient distracting clinical features in the emergence of diagnostic errors. BMJ Qual Saf 21:295-300
finding: Mechanism study. Reflection cuts errors caused by salient distracting features. Residents benefited, students did not.
numbers: Secondary analysis of 34 residents and 50 students, five internists coding errors. Residents: reflective 2.09 vs non-analytical 1.71 correct (P=0.03). Distractor-triggered errors 0.47 vs 0.85 (P=0.02). Students: no benefit.
limits: Secondary analysis of earlier data.
agent_relevance: Names a mechanism: the second look redirects attention from a seductive feature. Candidate check: which feature am I over-weighting.

source: Schmidt, van Gog, Schuit et al. (2017) Do patients' disruptive behaviours influence the accuracy of a doctor's diagnosis? BMJ Qual Saf 26:19-23
finding: Difficult-patient descriptions lowered accuracy. Deliberate reflection raised accuracy regardless of case complexity or patient behaviour.
numbers: N=63 family practice residents, six vignettes. Difficult 0.54 vs neutral 0.64 (P=0.017). Reflection raised 0.60 to 0.68 (P=0.002). Time to diagnose did not differ.
limits: Gain also held on simple cases, which contrasts with the 2008 finding.
agent_relevance: Difficulty gating is a prior, not a law.

source: Costa Filho, Moura, Brandao, Schmidt, Mamede (2019) Effects of deliberate reflection on diagnostic accuracy, confidence and diagnostic calibration in dermatology. Perspect Med Educ 8:230-236 [main result]
finding: Extension to a visual specialty. Final-year students diagnosed 12 skin images. Reflecting (supporting and opposing visual features, then two alternatives each with the same two lists) raised accuracy but not confidence or calibration.
numbers: N=61 (33 reflection, 28 control). Final accuracy 49.7 vs 38.4 percent, t(59)=3.33, p=0.002, d=0.84. Initial 45.96 vs 40.48 (d=0.42, p=0.10). Gain +3.79 vs -2.08 points (p=0.02). Confidence 64.29 vs 58.87 (p=0.21). Calibration 0.15 vs 0.20 (p=0.19).
limits: Systematic alternate-session allocation, not random. More women in reflection group (72.7 vs 42.9 percent). Students only. Images without history. 30 s for initial diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Reflection improves answers but not the confidence readout. Do not use post-reflection confidence as a pass signal (G3, G5).

source: Costa Filho, Moura, Brandao, Schmidt, Mamede (2019) Effects of deliberate reflection on diagnostic accuracy, confidence and diagnostic calibration in dermatology. Perspect Med Educ 8:230-236 [difficulty split]
finding: Reflection helped on the easier cases and only weakly on the harder ones. Overconfidence grew on hard cases (hard-easy effect).
numbers: Easier six cases: accuracy 76.8 vs 60.1 percent (p=0.004), calibration -0.08 vs 0.06 (p=0.016). Harder six: 22.7 vs 16.7 percent (p=0.080), confidence 59.3 vs 51.8 (p=0.131). Control estimated-vs-actual correct count r=0.285 (p=0.142).
limits: Difficulty defined post hoc from the sample's own performance.
agent_relevance: Fits the knowledge limit: gains come on cases within reach. Reflection does not rescue items far beyond the solver.

source: Mamede, van Gog, Moura et al. (2012) Reflection as a strategy to foster medical students' acquisition of diagnostic competence. Med Educ 46:464-472
finding: Learning effect with a delay. Practising cases with structured reflection hurt at once and helped a week later.
numbers: N=46 Year-4 students, six learning cases. Immediate test: reflection 0.48 vs differential 0.62 and immediate 0.61. One week later: reflection 0.66 vs 0.48 and 0.52. Interaction p=0.003. Reflection rose between tests (p=0.003) while the others fell.
limits: Delay one week; same diseases in tests.
agent_relevance: In a learning loop (stored lessons), reflection costs short-term and pays later. Do not judge a stored reflection by the next step's score.

source: Mamede, van Gog, Sampaio et al. (2014) How can students' diagnostic competence benefit most from practice with clinical cases? Acad Med 89:121-127
finding: Replicated and extended: reflection beat single-diagnosis and differential-diagnosis practice on new cases of practised diseases and on adjacent diseases.
numbers: N=110 Year-4 students. New exemplars: reflection 0.67, differential 0.51 (P=.014), single 0.36 (P<.001). New adjacent diseases: 0.44 vs 0.33 (P=.015) and 0.32 (P=.010). Single vs differential no difference. No group differences in the learning phase.
limits: One-week delay; vignettes.
agent_relevance: The for, against, missing table builds contrast knowledge between look-alikes. A plain differential does not.

source: Ibiapina, Mamede, Moura, Eloi-Santos, van Gog (2014) Effects of free, cued and modelled reflection on medical students' diagnostic competence. Med Educ 48:796-805
finding: Added guidance helped. Cued reflection (hypotheses supplied) and modelled reflection (expert's filled table) both beat free reflection.
numbers: N=58 Year-5 and 57 Year-6 students, eight learning cases. Modelled vs cued p=1.00; both beat free p<0.001. Condition p<0.001, year p=0.013, moment p=0.003.
limits: Advanced students. Examples felt less effortful. Possible expertise reversal for experts.
agent_relevance: If the hypothesis set comes from code or retrieval, reflection works better than letting the model free-generate alternatives (G5).

source: Mamede, Figueiredo-Soares, Santos, de Faria, Schmidt, van Gog (2019) Fostering novice students' diagnostic ability: the value of guiding deliberate reflection. Med Educ 53:628-637
finding: Replication with novices: cued reflection beat free reflection on studied diseases; modelled reflection fell in between. No effect on adjacent diseases (floor).
numbers: N=80 third-year students, nine learning cases, test two weeks later. Cued 0.58 (SD 0.23) vs free 0.41 (SD 0.20), p<0.02; modelled 0.54 (SD 0.22). Adjacent diseases: scores extremely low, no differences. Effort: cued and free similar, both more than studying examples (p<0.001).
limits: Transfer to adjacent diseases found in Acad Med 2014 did not replicate in novices.
agent_relevance: Reflection lessons do not transfer without knowledge.

source: Mamede, de Carvalho-Filho, de Faria et al. (2020) 'Immunising' physicians against availability bias in diagnostic reasoning: a randomised controlled experiment. BMJ Qual Saf 29:550-559
finding: Knowledge, not a reasoning procedure, protected against bias. One week of contrast practice with feedback on a disease cluster (diarrhoea or jaundice) made second-year residents resist a bias attempt on that cluster only.
numbers: N=91 residents, 8 hospitals, Brazil, 2017-18. Bias vignettes: immunised 0.40 vs 0.24 (diff 0.16, 95% CI 0.05-0.27, p=0.004). Non-bias vignettes 0.36 vs 0.41 (p=0.45). Non-immunised lost 0.17 under bias (p=0.005); immunised no loss (p=0.56).
limits: Disease-specific effect; simulated vignettes. Planned N of 98 was not reached. The paper says process-focused courses have largely failed to change performance.
agent_relevance: Content knowledge of discriminating features beats generic care instructions. Retrieve those features on the item.

source: Mamede, Goeijenbier, Schuit et al. (2021) Specific disease knowledge as predictor of susceptibility to availability bias in diagnostic reasoning. J Gen Intern Med 36:640-646
finding: Tests whether knowledge of discriminating features (speeded 2-second finding-disease decisions on 24 findings) predicts who succumbs to availability bias. The introduction notes a review that blamed only about 3 percent of errors on knowledge gaps, and argues knowledge and process cannot be separated.
numbers: Three-phase randomised design: four look-alike cases for each of hepatitis-IBD and AMI-encephalopathy, internal medicine residents. Outcome numbers were not extracted here.
limits: Intro and abstract read; results section not extracted.
agent_relevance: Separates knowledge failure from process failure, which tells when a second look can succeed.

source: Mamede, Hautz, Berendonk et al. (2020) Think Twice: Effects on diagnostic accuracy of returning to the case to reflect upon the initial diagnosis. Acad Med 95:1223-1229
finding: Key near-null for the content of reflection. Swiss physicians revised a diagnosis on difficult cases. All four revision types gave similar small gains, including a plain return to the case with no instructions.
numbers: N=167. Accuracy initial 0.22 vs final 0.26 overall, P<.001. Return only 0.21 to 0.23; confirmatory 0.24 to 0.31; contradictory 0.22 to 0.26; both 0.19 to 0.25. No significant group differences.
limits: Low base accuracy, so a gain of about 4 points. The 2023 review says this suggests alternatives to the time-consuming full procedure.
agent_relevance: Cost warning: a bare second look may carry most of the benefit. Any elaborate S5 loop must beat re-read then re-answer.

source: Ilgen, Bowen, McIntyre et al. (2013) Comparing diagnostic performance and the utility of clinical vignette-based assessment under testing conditions designed to encourage either automatic or analytic thought. Acad Med 88:1545-1551
finding: Failed replication of a benefit from analytic instruction. 393 clinicians gave first impressions or followed a directed search (three diagnoses, then supporting and non-supporting features). No accuracy difference.
numbers: N=393 (students, trainees, faculty). Instruction F(1,379)=2.44, P=.12. Complexity F=965.2. Experience F=39.6.
limits: Mamede and Schmidt (2014) reply that DR needs hypotheses to arise one by one from evidence, but Ilgen asked for a competing list first.
agent_relevance: Order matters: a rival list up front is not the same as falsifying a held hypothesis step by step.

source: Norman, Sherbino, Dore et al. (2014) The etiology of diagnostic errors: a controlled trial of system 1 versus system 2 reasoning. Acad Med 89:277-284
finding: Telling residents to be slow, careful and reflective instead of fast did not raise accuracy. Time rose, accuracy did not.
numbers: N=96 (Speed, 2010) and 108 (Reflect, 2011) second-year residents, 20 cases. Accuracy 44.5 vs 45.0 percent. 69 s vs 89 s per case (P<.001). Incorrect cases took 17 s longer.
limits: Different cohorts in different years, so not randomised. Instruction only, no structured steps.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to think carefully is not a second look. Compute must go to a structured check (G1, G2).

source: Sherbino, Kulasegaram, Howey, Norman (2014) Ineffectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies to reduce biases in diagnostic reasoning: a controlled trial. CJEM 16:34-40
finding: Cognitive forcing training did not reduce search-satisficing or availability errors in novices.
numbers: N=191 (145 cognitive forcing training, 46 control), computer cases at end of 4-week emergency rotation. Search-satisficing cases: searched for a second diagnosis 52% vs 48% (p=0.91); found it 54% vs 48% (p=0.13). False-positive cases: invented a second diagnosis 64% vs 77% (p=0.12). Availability-bias cases: found the uncommon diagnosis 45% in both groups (p=0.98).
limits: Full text read this session. Groups unbalanced. Training taught bias awareness, not a disease-knowledge re-examination.
agent_relevance: Forced-doubt rules without content knowledge fail, in line with G1.

source: Kulatunga-Moruzi, Brooks, Norman (2011) Teaching posttraining: influencing diagnostic strategy with instructions at test. J Exp Psychol Appl 17:195-209
finding: Dual instructions at the moment of diagnosis (similarity-based first, then apply rules) improved accuracy. Applying rules first inhibited later similarity-based reasoning.
numbers: Typicality effect indexes analytic processing; similarity effect indexes similarity-based processing. Study numbers were not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Medical students.
agent_relevance: Fast guess first, then rule-based check, is the sequence that worked (S1 then S8).

source: Myung, Kang, Phyo, Shin, Park (2013) Effect of enhanced analytic reasoning on diagnostic accuracy: a randomized controlled study. Med Teach 35:248-250
finding: Randomised OSCE with standardised patients: listing differentials and findings compatible or not compatible with each before diagnosing raised accuracy in fourth-year students.
limits: The list came before the diagnosis, so it is not a second look at a held hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Shows benefit with live standardised patients, beyond paper vignettes.

source: Prakash, Sladek, Schuwirth (2019) Interventions to improve diagnostic decision making: a systematic review and meta-analysis on reflective strategies. Med Teach 41:517-524
finding: Meta-analysis of guided reflection: positive pooled effect. Review covered 44 studies with 4380 medical professionals, 2000-2016.
numbers: Guided reflection effect size 0.38 (95% CI 0.23-0.52), p<0.001. Immediate feedback and modelled reflection also promising.
limits: Methodological issues blocked pooling for other strategies. Search ended 2016.
agent_relevance: Best older pooled estimate: moderate, from heterogeneous tasks.

source: Staal, Hooftman, Gunput, Mamede, Frens, van den Broek, Alsma, Zwaan (2022) Effect on diagnostic accuracy of cognitive reasoning tools for the workplace setting: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Qual Saf 31:899-910
finding: Pooled all workplace reasoning tools (13 checklists, 12 guided reflection, 2 decision support, 2 instructions at test). Small effect. No factor (intervention type, case difficulty, expertise) explained larger gains.
numbers: 29 studies, N=2732. Hedges g=0.20 (95% CI 0.10-0.29), p<0.001 after removing three training studies; I2 fell from 70 to 38 percent. 17 of 29 (59 percent) were verification after an initial diagnosis.
limits: Only 2 of 29 were in real clinical practice. 13 of 29 let participants see the same cases, so a mere revisit effect is mixed in.
agent_relevance: Realistic expectation is g near 0.2, not large. A second look is worth doing when cheap, not as a cure.

source: Mamede & Schmidt (2023) Deliberate reflection and clinical reasoning: Founding ideas and empirical findings. Med Educ 57:76-85 [failed instruction types]
finding: Instructions to be more analytic, to consider all findings before concluding, or to watch for misleading information did not help and sometimes hurt. A tentative hypothesis must exist first, then repair works.
numbers: Cited: Kulatunga-Moruzi 2011, Norman 2014, Arzy 2009. Cognitive forcing and general debiasing checklists show little or no effect; content-focused checklists help (Kammer 2021, Shimizu 2013).
limits: Review by the lab that promotes DR; but consistent with the independent nulls above.
agent_relevance: Order: first answer, then audit. Not audit while answering (G1, G2).

source: Mamede & Schmidt (2023) Deliberate reflection and clinical reasoning: Founding ideas and empirical findings. Med Educ 57:76-85 [mechanisms]
finding: Three candidate mechanisms: (1) fuller activation of prior disease knowledge, (2) reprocessing the case under each new hypothesis, (3) stronger links between disease and findings, giving better look-alike contrast. None tested directly.
numbers: Ribeiro 2019: DR group recalled 40 percent more propositions of a 1200-word text than the differential group. The effect held under restricted time, so it is partly cognitive, not only motivation.
limits: Authors call the explanations tentative. No evidence that DR training changes a general reasoning style.
agent_relevance: S5 should force re-retrieval of knowledge about each hypothesis, not just re-read the answer.

source: Eye-tracking experiment on selective processing of clinical information in correct and incorrect diagnoses (2025). Med Educ (PMC11976213)
finding: What a successful revision looks like. Residents who received a wrong suggestion and revised to the correct diagnosis looked longer and more often at information relevant to the correct diagnosis.
numbers: N=19 residents, 12 cases (half with correct suggestion, half incorrect). Dwell time 6.3 s (SD 5.1) vs about 4 s elsewhere. Fixations 25 (SD 20) vs 16-17. Time to diagnose 86 s (SD 47) with an incorrect suggestion vs 70 s. Confidence 64-67 percent whatever the accuracy.
limits: Tiny N. Case-specific knowledge seems the key, not selective attention alone.
agent_relevance: Revision succeeds when attention shifts to evidence for the alternative; confidence carries no signal about success (G3, G5).

source: Teaching medical students to apply deliberate reflection (2023/24, PMC10841076)
finding: Can DR be learned and used unprompted? Students who practised DR recalled more features for the alternative diagnosis one week later, whether or not the case was described as difficult.
numbers: N=119 students, six test cases with two likely diagnoses. Alternative-diagnosis features recalled p=.013. Features of the provided diagnosis p=.004 on first three cases; no difference on the last three described as difficult.
limits: Feature recall is a proxy for reflection, not accuracy. Telling students a case is hard did not change reflection.
agent_relevance: A habit of looking at the alternative can be trained by scaffold, not by a hint of difficulty.

source: Learning deliberate reflection in medical diagnosis: does learning-by-teaching help? (2023). Adv Health Sci Educ (PMID 35913665)
finding: Failed transfer. 56 GP residents studied DR examples and explained them to a fictitious peer on video; at test 1 to 3 weeks later they reflected and diagnosed no better than controls.
numbers: Accuracy p=.263; time p=.598; mental effort p=.544; confidence p=.710; contradiction units p=.544.
limits: Maybe controls also reflected, or the taught group did not use the method.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a taught method is used at test. Build it into the program, not the model's habits.

source: Effects of case revisitation during deliberate reflection on medical students' diagnostic accuracy: a randomized experiment (2026). Diagnosis (PMID 42644626)
finding: Boundary condition on the second look. Reflecting without the case text helped accuracy on studied diseases; reflecting with the text helped transfer to adjacent diseases.
numbers: N=67 Brazilian year 3-4 students, 15-day delay. Group by disease type chi2(1)=7.68, p=0.006. Studied diseases OR=1.77 (p=0.050) favouring no access. Adjacent OR=0.56 (p=0.050) favouring access. No overall difference.
limits: Borderline p values, one lab.
agent_relevance: Whether the checker sees the raw case or only its own summary changes what is learned. Choose by purpose (G3).

source: Comparing faded examples and cued reflection in teaching diagnostic reasoning (2026) (PMID 41943587)
finding: Two scaffolds gave equal accuracy in sixth-year students, consistent with expertise reversal.
numbers: 70 students, 59 completed. Accuracy at test p=.99. Confidence predicts accuracy OR=1.18 (p=.02). Recall of correct propositions OR=1.10 (p=.005).
limits: One lab, small, advanced students.
agent_relevance: At higher competence, less guidance is no worse.

source: Mamede, Rikers, Schmidt et al. (2008) Influence of perceived difficulty of cases on physicians' diagnostic reasoning. Acad Med
finding: Doctors shift to reflective mode when a case is perceived as problematic. Telling them others failed the case raised accuracy, slowed their concept judgements, and increased time and inferences in think-aloud.
numbers: Experiment 1: 20 residents, 10 cases. Experiment 2: 18 residents, 2 cases, think-aloud. Accuracy higher in the problematic context.
limits: Manipulation was a statement that others failed the case.
agent_relevance: A difficulty signal triggers real extra analysis. A code-counted difficulty signal is a legitimate S5 trigger (G1).

source: Self-explanation and structured reflection: layered analysis (2021). Perspect Med Educ (PMC8187699)
finding: Conceptual paper that spells out the philosophy, principles and techniques of self-explanation and structured reflection so they can be implemented without losing their core.
numbers: No outcome data.
limits: No effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Names the two transferable methods and their core principles.

source: Conscious versus unconscious thinking in the medical domain: the deliberation-without-attention effect examined (2014) (PMC4078052)
finding: Failed replication of deliberation-without-attention. Unconscious thought was no better than conscious thought for survival estimates.
numbers: N=143 (86 physicians, 57 students), four fictitious 60-year-old patients, 12 (complex) or 4 (simple) categories, 8 s per statement. Experts better than students. No conscious versus unconscious difference and no interaction.
limits: Different task (prognosis) than diagnosis.
agent_relevance: No evidence that sleeping on it beats an explicit recheck.

source: Lambe, Hevey, Kelly (2018) Guided Reflection Interventions Show No Effect on Diagnostic Accuracy in Medical Students. Front Psychol 9:2297
finding: Failed replication. Short (2 alternatives) and long (6 alternatives) guided reflection gave no better final diagnoses than first impressions in senior students. Reflection did raise the accuracy of the list of alternatives, which is partly a counting effect.
numbers: N=186 fourth/fifth-year students, fictional cases. Final diagnosis (strict) F(2,173)=0.841 p>0.05. Alternatives named: long 3.03 vs short 1.86 (t(61.92)=6.76). Accuracy of the alternatives list (lenient): short 0.70, long 0.72, control 0.47, F(2,175)=18.99 eta2=0.18. Confidence change short 0.11, long 0.10 (ns). Pre-reflection confidence higher in long group (3.15 vs 2.79).
limits: Cases hard (low accuracy) but not structurally complex: no secondary diagnosis. Students only. Authors say novices may already reason analytically.
agent_relevance: Asking for more alternatives raises coverage, not final accuracy. Score the final answer, not the candidate list. The second look should be gated (G1) and checked against evidence (G2).

source: Monteiro, Sherbino, Patel, Mazzetti, Norman, Howey (2015) Reflecting on Diagnostic Errors: Taking a Second Look is Not Enough. J Gen Intern Med 30:1270-4
finding: When residents themselves chose which cases to revise, they revised few, mostly the ones they got wrong, and fixed only a small share. A free second look barely helps because the missing thing is knowledge.
numbers: N=47 residents (19 PGY1, 11 PGY2, 17 PGY3), 16 cases, pass 1 mean 26 min. Only 60 of 745 diagnoses (8%) revised. Score 1.20 to 1.22 of 2 (t=2.15 p=0.03). Revised items were weaker at pass 1 (0.64 vs 1.25 of 2, p<0.001). Pass-1 accuracy 58-64%. Only 18% of incorrect diagnoses were revised to correct. Six correct diagnoses revised after reflection fell about 0.8. Case read time 97 s in pass 1, 17 s in pass 2.
limits: Self-directed, no prescribed procedure, written cases. Contrasts with the prescribed, structured procedure in Mamede 2008/2010.
agent_relevance: Self-triggered revision has low recall and some damage to right answers. Gate revision with a detected signal and require the revision to cite evidence (G1, G2). Keep the original answer unless the check supports a change.

source: Chernikova, Heitzmann, Stadler, Holzberger, Seidel, Fischer (2019/2020) Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education: a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education. Educ Psychol Rev
finding: Across 35 diagnostic-competence interventions, scaffolds that include reflection phases worked about twice as well as scaffolds without them, and best for advanced learners.
numbers: Reflection phases g=0.58 (SE 0.11) vs no reflection phases g=0.26 (SE 0.11); moderator Q(1,31)=17.11 p<0.001. Advanced learners with reflection phases g=0.67 (SE 0.23); examples instead of problem solving for high-prior-knowledge learners g=0.18 (ns).
limits: Educational outcomes in medicine and teacher education, mixed designs. Not a test of in-the-moment error correction.
agent_relevance: Reflection pays when the solver already has knowledge. Pair with retrieval for weak solvers.
